news.casting_brief: Downwind residents, ED nurses and physicians, county public health officials, UCLA epidemiologists, gas facility operators; tension between exposed families and slow institutional response.
news.script_brief: A 112-day uncontrolled gas blowout drives a surge in ED visits downwind. As researchers track respiratory infections, GI symptoms, and stress disorders, residents demand answers while the spike persists a year later. Beats: the leak, the rush to care, the data reveal, the lingering toll, the call for facility safety.
news.news_close_brief: Emergency visits rose sharply downwind of the Aliso Canyon gas blowout and stayed elevated a year later, researchers found, underscoring the need to safeguard communities near natural gas storage facilities.
key_terms: UCLA Aliso Canyon Disaster Health Research Study
Los Angeles County Department of Public Health

dramatic_state.dramatic_question: Will Barney make the UCLA Aliso Canyon Disaster Health Research Study's data force facility safety reforms before the case is quietly closed?
dramatic_state.character_a_wants: To close the Aliso Canyon case, calling the air safe so the gas storage facility reopens.
dramatic_state.character_b_wants: Force release of the UCLA study data proving the blowout's lingering toll, and shut the facility.
dramatic_state.ending_change: Pourat's data confirms the year-long ED-visit spike from hazardous air pollutants, forcing safety hearings instead of a quiet reopening.

rendered_lines: For one hundred and twelve days the air itself turned against them, and tonight we follow the breath, the fear, and the answers a downwind town still demands.

Third tower's still venting since midnight, and the board's lit up like Christmas - forty calls in since I poured this coffee, and it's gone cold in my hand. Same words every time: throats, headaches, kids that won't stop coughing on the east side.
You log forty, Barney, and I'll show you the sixty we dropped while you were saying it... we're writing names on a pad that fills up faster than I can turn the page.

We staffed this room for a bad weekend - three girls, two lines, a coffee urn that quits by ten. That was the plan when somebody drew it up, and nobody's looked at the plan since. Last hour we crossed nine hundred, Ren, and the count doesn't tire the way we do.

You can hear it out there still - that hiss off the third tower, soft, like a kettle nobody'll lift. They tell me there's a cap coming, and I believe them, I do... but my boy's been coughing into his pillow three nights now, and a cap won't pull what's already in the ground out of his lungs come spring.
Musical interlude bridging setup into the next phase.

Look at the pad - every name on it's from the ridge, the high streets, folks whose phones still catch a signal. The east side, the low end under that hiss? Dead air. We're counting the ones who can reach us and calling it the whole town, when the worst of it can't get a tone to dial out on.

There's the relay line down in the basement - old county trunk, never decommissioned. I throw the overflow onto that and we stop dropping sixty an hour... but it won't carry the east exchange. Those few from the low end still squeaking through to us - they go quiet the second I flip it.

Don't touch it. Pull that folder - the red tab, the collapse list. Every address marked for crews first is east of the towers, down in the dead air. You flip your relay and you save the count, Ren... and you hang up on the only ones we put on paper to save.

I'm walking the trucks off the ridge - all of them, every unit that can roll downhill. Read me the red-tab addresses, Martin, top to bottom, and don't slow down when I don't answer, because I'll be moving pins while you talk.

Ren. Ren, hold your hand a second - the ridge board just lit. Four calls, same street, all of 'em saying the same word, and your trucks are halfway down the hill with their backs to it... we didn't trade one for the other. We bought a second pile.

Then you find me a fifth truck, Barney, because I've got two streets full of people on paper and one set of wheels, and the math says I pick a corner to be wrong on - so look at the pad, look at it, and tell me which name we cross off while it's still talking.
Musical interlude bridging complication into the next phase.

There's no fifth truck, Martin, there never was - I called the depot twice and the dispatcher let it ring. So here's the pad as it stands: forty-one names with a check beside 'em, and these nine down the bottom... I've got my pencil on 'em, no mark, just the wet spot where I've been holding it too long.

Don't cross 'em off - turn the page over and copy the nine onto a fresh sheet. We didn't lose those names tonight, Barney. We carry them. That sheet rides in the truck till morning, and somebody answers for it that isn't you.

Read me the time off the clock and write it at the top, Barney - fold Ren's nine inside the logbook where the binding still holds, and we don't burn that ledger, not next spring, not ever; somebody comes asking in five years, the page is there waiting with the lamp still on.

Hundred and twelve nights I've sharpened this same stub down to my knuckles... funny thing, the cough doesn't quit when the trucks come back up the hill - so leave the lamp, Martin, I'll be the one sitting under it.
The air over Aliso Canyon has stilled, yet a year on the sickness lingers and the visits climb, reminding us that those who live beside such storehouses deserve to breathe without fear.
